chore(plugin-template): give the e2e config a secret long enough for encrypted fields

The 10-byte PAYLOAD_SECRET fails Payload's init in any plugin that stores a
value through encryptedField, which is how the webhooks e2e job failed.

docs(webhooks): allowlist, retention, drafts on autosave collections, reserved transport headers

Also corrects two lines the code had moved past: inline deliveries are sent
together rather than sequentially, and the reserved header list is no longer
six names.

fix(webhooks): host allowlist, log retention, and a second hardening pass

New options:
- delivery.allowedHosts: an opt-in hostname allowlist (exact or *.example.com),
  enforced on save, at startup for code subscriptions, and at delivery time.
  Entries that are not bare hostnames fail at startup.
- deliveriesLog.retentionDays and an exported pruneDeliveries(): finished
  deliveries past the window are deleted, at most once an hour after an event.

Fixes:
- an autosave collection no longer emits created for the empty draft the admin
  makes on "Create new" (a Local API draft create with a user); REST, GraphQL
  and user-less Local API creates still emit
- a source slug that matches no registered collection, or that is one of the
  plugin's own or Payload's internal collections, throws at startup
- the redeliver endpoint returns the outcome and the button reports it; a
  replay that is going nowhere is refused before it is queued
- inline deliveries for one write are sent together, with results written one
  at a time; a send that throws marks its row dead
- Host, Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Keep-Alive, Upgrade and Expect are
  reserved header names
- encryptExistingSecrets also seals legacy header values, and reports a row
  that fails to save by id instead of stopping the run
- the URL and header-name validators no longer judge a value the write is not
  changing, so a rule added after a row was stored cannot block saving,
  rotating or disabling that row; the delivery path still enforces it

fix(webhooks): keep legacy header values, use the message id in the body, trim header names

- a header value stored before encryption reads back as it is and is sealed on
  the next save, instead of reading as null and being wiped by that save
- the body's id is the same msg_ id as the webhook-id header; a redelivery is
  restamped with its own
- header names are stored and sent trimmed; code subscriptions with an invalid
  header name or a line break in a value fail at startup
- docs: re-save subscriptions with headers before dropping an encryption key,
  since rotateEncryptedFields does not reach array fields; an admin create
  without Generate needs a rotation to get a copyable secret

Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/main' into plugin/dedupe

# Conflicts:
#	pnpm-lock.yaml

docs(dedupe): correct what the docs got wrong

- The `union` example sets the policy on a list, the only kind it
  applies to; a textarea fell back to `nonEmpty`.
- On Postgres a `required` reference to a merged-in document fails the
  merge's delete, wherever it comes from; an optional one is cleared.
- A pointer at a document of the merge is removed only from optional
  fields the reviewer may update.
- The audit example stores the snapshots whole, hidden fields included.
- The score's formula, `key: false`, the refusal for `update` on a
  document going to the trash, when `pair.found` fires again, and what
  `compose` may name.

docs(dedupe): check for duplicates before saving

The plugin no longer checks the edit form itself. A new page shows the
pieces for a check of your own: `findDuplicates`, the check endpoint
and `useDuplicateCheck`, and a guided create form built on them with
@10x-media/form-variants. The dev app runs that form as a `guided`
variant of its customers, and an e2e test drives it.

The README links to the page, and its links lose a `/docs` the docs
site does not have.

fix(dedupe): close pairs on unpublish, log a failed check on save

A document taken off publication now leaves its open pairs, as one in
the trash does; its "Not duplicates" marks stay. Under
`disableJobsQueue` a check on save that fails, such as on an adapter
that is down, is logged instead of failing the save. It still runs
inside the save's transaction, so a save that rolls back leaves no
pair behind.

feat(dedupe): build an adapter on the plugin's comparisons

`comparePresets` exports the built-in comparisons, for a compare of
your own such as one that reads ü as ue. The docs say what an
adapter's `index` and `remove` run inside, and how an outside index
stays in step: the Typesense example writes at once, outside the
save's transaction, and queues a check job that puts a rollback right.

feat(dedupe): match names with a typo

`typos: true` on a `compare: 'text'` match field adds blocking keys
that meet a word of four letters or more with one letter wrong,
missing or extra: "Jhon" and "John". Off by default, as it adds a key
per letter; the keys adapter reads them side by side outside a
transaction.

A name with a word the other lacks no longer scores as the same name:
"Anna" and "Anna Schmidt" are similar, not equal.

perf(dedupe): score each pair once in a scan, write keys together

A scan scored a pair again in every bucket its two documents shared.
A pair met in an earlier bucket is now skipped (Comparison
Propagation, as in Papadakis et al.).

Outside a transaction a scan indexes ten documents at once, each with a
request of its own, and the keys adapter writes a document's keys
together. Inside one they stay sequential: a transaction runs one
command at a time.

feat(dedupe): show a group larger than one merge

The queue shows each group's size, as `7, up to 5 per merge` when it
holds more than `maxGroupSize`. The merge screen counts the similar
documents it leaves out, which stay in the queue.

feat(dedupe): show unpublished changes of a merged-in document

A document whose latest version is a draft over what it published is
marked Changed on the merge screen, as Payload marks it. When merged-in
documents are deleted, the screen warns that such changes go with them.

fix(dedupe): keep the merged-in documents without a transaction

Without a transaction, a merge that failed after the merged-in
documents gave up their unique values left them with placeholders. A
failure before the primary is written now puts their values back; a
value that cannot be put back is logged.

A merged-in document that can hold neither a placeholder nor an empty
value for a unique value the primary takes is deleted before the
primary is written. Without a transaction such a merge is now refused,
and the merge screen says so before the click, in either `absorbed`
mode.

A unique value in rows the primary takes is now replaced in place, in
its locale, as one at the top level is, instead of deleting the
document.

feat(dedupe): search the queue, laid out as a list view

- A search bar as the list view's. It finds a group by any of its
  documents, through the collection's list search
  (`listSearchableFields`, else the title field) under the reader's
  access. The collection filter sits in the bar.
- What a status means sits under the title, as a list's description.
- A tab's count stands apart from its label and shows on the active
  tab too, as the Versions tab's does.
- A collection filter is a breadcrumb of its own; the merge screen's
  crumbs lead back to it.
- The page ends with the list view's padding.
- A merge link with a document that is gone, in the trash or not
  readable leads to the queue of its collection, which says "not
  found" as the admin does. An error on the merge screen loses its
  "Back to duplicates" button: the breadcrumbs lead back.
- A group marked not duplicates leaves its tab while one of its
  documents is in the trash, and is back once it is restored.

feat(dedupe): the merge screen as the admin draws it

- A document's name opens it in a new tab, and an edit button beside
  it opens a drawer, as an upload field shows its document.
- Rows of arrays and blocks carry the label the document's form gives
  them: the collection's own row label, or Payload's, with a block's
  number, type and name.
- A row's check keeps its whole focus glow.
- A value that differs from the primary is marked word by word.
- The radio or check of a value sits in a square before it.
- "Only differences" and "Highlight differences" sit in the footer,
  smaller, beside the buttons.
- A group marked not duplicates is reopened before it can be merged:
  its footer holds Reopen instead of Not duplicates and Merge.
- The column heads line up with the fields below them.
- The tenant row shows the value alone: the multi-tenant field's own
  component selected its tenant for the whole admin.

feat(dedupe): name a field as the list filter does

A field inside groups and tabs was labelled by its path, `Profile /
Extra`, on a grey line of its own. The merge screen and its refusals
now name it as the list view's filter does: the labels of the groups,
named tabs and collapsibles it sits in, then its own, translated, as
`Customer profile > Rating > Score`.

The dev app's customers carry such labels.

fix(dedupe): drop what still spoke of removed parts

The merge record, the plugin's own sidebar and its moving of references
are gone, but the merge screen's notes and its confirmation still said
the merge record kept the originals, and comments still named the
record, the history, the sidebar and moved references.

fix(webhooks): boot the e2e app and register the encrypted editor strings

The e2e server never started: PAYLOAD_SECRET in the Playwright config was 10
bytes, and @10x-media/fields refuses to derive encryption keys from less than
16, so Payload's init threw and every test past the first failed against an
empty admin. The earlier build failure had been hiding this.

With the app booting, two more things showed up:
- the write-only editor rendered raw translation keys (fields:generateValue),
  because its strings are registered by the fields() plugin, which a consumer
  of this plugin does not have to install. They are merged here, under the
  host's own translations.
- the rotation spec asserted a value on the date field's wrapper instead of
  its input.

The Playwright config also gains the env-boundary lint ignore the template
and the other plugins carry.

docs(webhooks): document the access default, drafts, header encryption and overrides

Covers the admin-collection access default, redeliver deferring to read
access, autosave and includeDrafts, encrypted custom header values, the
subscriptionSource column, redirect and response-size handling, and what an
override can and cannot replace. The changeset carries the same list.

fix(webhooks): address the review round and harden dispatch

Review must-fixes and should-fixes:
- add every new translation key to all ten locales, and replace the stale
  secret help text in each
- overrides.endpoints and overrides.admin.components now add to the plugin's
  endpoints and document controls instead of replacing them; the write-only
  response strip runs after the override
- rotating a subscription that does not exist returns 404
- Escape no longer dismisses the reveal dialog holding the only copy of a
  rotated secret

Smaller review items:
- Rotate secret and Redeliver move into the document controls; Redeliver
  confirms first
- the secret hint is shown read-only on an existing subscription and cannot be
  rewritten through the API
- an unsealed stored secret is refused even when it is already canonical whsec_
- the subscription URL must be absolute http(s) without embedded credentials
- collections is typed against CollectionSlug
- the no-transaction warning gives adapter-appropriate advice
- the dev seed uses a fixed secret and the dev sink verifies with standardwebhooks

Found in a second pass:
- both collections default to users of admin.user rather than any logged-in user
- redeliver defers to the deliveries collection's read access
- autosaves no longer emit; includeDrafts: false stops deliberate draft saves too
- a throw while dispatching, a consumer transform included, no longer fails
  the write; transform runs once per event before any delivery row exists
- deliveries record subscriptionSource, so a code subscription id cannot shadow
  a collection row id
- custom header values are encrypted at rest and masked in the admin; a value
  with a line break is rejected
- deliveries do not follow redirects and read at most 2,000 response characters
- a queued job shares the write's transaction
- a MongoDB WriteConflict during rotation maps to 409

feat(dedupe): show fields with their own component as the form does

A field with its own `admin.components.Field` was drawn as a bare value:
a rating as `4`, a color as `#ff8800`. A group drawn as one input, such
as a phone, was split into its fields, so a merge could take the country
from one document and the number from another, and offered fields the
component keeps to itself. A list drawn by its own component had no
check to pick it with.

Such a field is now drawn on the merge screen by its own component,
read-only and inert, and picked as one value. A group or list with one
is merged whole; `dedupeCustom({ split: true })` merges it part by part
as before. A match field may read a field inside such a group. A cell
whose value differs from the primary's is marked, since no diff can be
drawn inside a component.

feat(dedupe): write a merge in a locale the primary is complete in

The values every locale shares were always written in the default
locale, so a primary filled in German only could not be merged: Payload
checks the locale it writes, and English was empty. A collection now
takes `writeLocale`, a code or a function of the survivor such as its
tenant's language. Without it, the default locale is used when the
survivor holds every required value there, else the first locale it
does. A code the config has no locale for stops the app at startup.

On a collection with drafts, a locale whose missing required values the
survivor already lacked is written as a draft and published with the
write locale, which Payload checks alone. The merge leaves it as
incomplete as it found it instead of refusing.

The dev app writes its customers in the language of their office.

refactor(dedupe): no merge record, the hook gets what it held

The dedupe-merges collection is gone, with `overrides.merges`, its
statuses and `mergeId` in the apply result and the merge events.
`hooks.beforeRemove` now receives the merged-in documents as they were,
before their unique values were released, and the merge decisions: a
host keeps its own record there. A failed merge is logged and sent as
`merge.failed`.

The merge's transaction now starts on a single command before the
hook: on MongoDB a hook beginning with a paginated find sent its count
beside it and found no transaction.

The dev app records each merge with @10x-media/audit-logs, and its e2e
script builds every workspace package the dev app imports.

feat(dedupe): a beforeRemove hook to move references

The plugin no longer moves references to the merged-in documents.
`hooks.beforeRemove` runs once per merge, with the merge's request,
before the first of them is trashed or deleted: on Postgres a delete
takes the references along, so the move has to come first. Throwing
fails the merge and rolls it back where the database opens a
transaction.

The dev app moves its customers' orders and trips on it, and the docs
show the same code.

refactor(dedupe): cut what the review asked to remove

The plugin finds duplicates and merges them; the rest is the host's.

- Reference repointing: the preview, the move, the "Linked from" counts,
  the `references` option and the `repointed` field. `withoutOwn` stays.
- The merge history views and the queue's Merged tab. The merges
  collection is still written, as a record without UI.
- The plugin's own sidebar links and `view.navLabel` / `view.history`.
- The superseded and stale pair states: a pair whose document is gone,
  merged or trashed, or that no longer qualifies, is deleted.
- The summary line under a row's label on the merge screen; an empty
  list of rows is now one single-line row tall.
- The duplicate check on forms: DuplicatesField, the confirm buttons,
  registerFormWarnings and the `form` option. findDuplicates, the check
  endpoint and useDuplicateCheck stay.

The dev app places its own sidebar link to the queue.

chore(dedupe): one file per dev collection

The dev app kept fourteen collections and a global in one file, and the
custom-field showcase at its root. Each collection now has a file under
dev/collections, as in the other plugins' dev apps, and the global one under
dev/globals. Nothing else changes.

feat(dedupe): scope tenancy by the multi-tenant plugin's collections

A collection counted as tenant-scoped when it had a field named like the
tenant field, and tenantOf read that field on any document. A collection
whose `tenant` field means something else had its keys prefixed, its pairs
kept apart and its merges refused by it.

`multiTenancy.collections` takes the multi-tenant plugin's own object: only
those collections are scoped, and without it the field name decides as
before. tenantOf takes the collection and is null in one it does not scope,
the tenant field is held to the survivor only where scoped, and a collection
marked `isGlobal` is refused at startup.

The dev app passes one object to both plugins and adds a `staff` collection
whose `tenant` field is a branch, with an adapter of its own.

fix(dedupe): index on every save, whatever checkOnSave says

`checkOnSave: false` skipped the index together with the pairs, so with the
keys adapter a document saved since the last scan had no keys and
findDuplicates could not find it. A document taken off publication also
stayed in the index. Every save of a matched collection now keeps the index
current; `checkOnSave` decides only whether the save looks for pairs.
Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin' into feat/hmac-standard-plus-encrypt-rest

feat(dedupe): a threshold per findDuplicates call

The collection's `match.minScore` was the only threshold, so a check before
creating could not ask for weaker matches than the queue keeps. findDuplicates
takes `minScore` for one call, and the check endpoint and useDuplicateCheck
pass it on. A value outside 0 to 1 is refused with a 400.

feat(dedupe): an adapter per collection

A project that wanted its own index for one collection and the keys for the
rest had to branch on the collection in every adapter method. A collection
now takes `adapter: (base) => adapter`, given the plugin's adapter, and the
one it returns is used whole for that collection. The plugin's `adapter`
stays the default.

Every adapter is checked for `findCandidates` at startup, `adapter` on a

docs(content-lock): document kv failures and job deferral while lock state is unreadable

Timing now explains how servers share the windows through the kv snapshot,
that a server whose rebuilt snapshot cannot be stored enforces the windows it
read from the collection, that saving or deleting a window fails while its
snapshot cannot be stored, and when writes are rejected. The jobs page adds
the queue pause and the one-minute deferral while the state cannot be read.

perf(content-lock): share one lock state read across concurrent callers

Payload resolves admin permissions with Promise.all over every collection
and operation, and each wrapped create, update and delete reads the lock
state. One admin page load after the 2 s memory TTL issued about 150
concurrent kv reads, and after the 60 s snapshot age about 150 collection
reads and kv writes. Concurrent callers for one Payload instance now share
one read and at most one rebuild. A failed read rejects the callers that
shared it and is dropped, so the next call starts over. A window write
replaces the process memory just before its kv write, so a read that began
before the write cannot store its older windows over it.

fix(content-lock): retry jobs stopped by unreadable lock state after a minute

A job interrupted while the lock state could not be read carries a
ContentLockedError that names no window. It was deferred for the 24 h bound
of a window without an end, and nothing released it early: only a window
change or the heal path does, and both work from window ids. A scheduled
publish that ran during a kv blip went out a day late. Such a job now runs
again after a minute. Windows without an end keep the 24 h bound, which
"End now" cuts short.

fix(content-lock): stop locking everything when snapshot kv write fails

A reader that finds the kv snapshot missing or stale rebuilds it from the
collection. When the kv write failed, the error escaped getContentLockState
and readStateOrLocked failed closed, locking everything although the windows
had been read. The rebuild now logs the failed write and still returns and
holds the windows. A window write still throws on a failed kv write, so it
never reports a change other servers cannot see.

fix(fields): land the phone field feedback round and quality sweep (#219)

* fix(fields): refuse impossible and over-long phone input

The character rule was only consulted, never enforced: `formatDraft` returned
input it had just rejected. It now refuses the keystroke and puts the caret back
where the refused characters would have gone, since leaving state unchanged
re-renders nothing.

Entry also grows without bound today. It now stops at the country's own ceiling
where libphonenumber defines one, and at E.164's fifteen digits otherwise, which
is the only bound several countries have. Digits spend that budget, so
formatting costs nothing, and a bulk paste still lands so blur salvage can read
a real number out of it.

* fix(fields): let a picked country survive the commit that follows it

Picking a country on a stored number did nothing, because the commit re-read
the country off the number: `+1 212 555 2368` under Canada parses back as the
United States, and that answer overwrote the pick. An explicit pick now settles
the country, while a typed or pasted number keeps deriving its own.

The pick also has to outrank the stored country, since e164 storage has no
country column and re-reads it off the number. It steps aside again the moment
a commit derives a country, so it answers for one number rather than becoming a
mode the field is stuck in.

* feat(fields): resolve the phone country from the calling code as it is typed

The country came only from a complete valid number, so typing `+41` left the
flag on the old one until the whole line parsed. Two questions were being asked
as one: which calling code this is, answerable from `+41` on sight, and which
country within it, which needs more digits.

The calling code now settles immediately and adopts its main country, which the
existing validated read still refines as area-code digits arrive: `+7 7` becomes
Kazakhstan, `+1 604 555 1234` becomes Canada. Junk carrying no calling code
still names no country. libphonenumber exposes no accessor for the
code-to-countries map, so the metadata shape is read directly and pinned by a
test, the way KNOWN_COUNTRY_CODES already is.

Picking a country now sheds the draft's calling code even when the draft is too
short to parse, or the code left behind would name the old country straight back.

* perf(fields): key the phone country list on its contents

Payload re-deserializes clientProps on every server form-state round trip, so a
`countries` or `preferredCountries` allowlist arrives as a new array with the
same entries and invalidates the memo. Each invalidation rebuilt the whole
localized, sorted country list. Typing four characters into one showcase field
ran 980 Intl.DisplayNames lookups; it now runs none.

* feat(fields): rename phone preferredCountries to priorityCountries and add a heading label

Review feedback: the picker's pinned-country group heading read "Frequently
used" for a list that was never automatic, only ever the explicit
preferredCountries option. The mechanism was fine; the wording implied usage
tracking that doesn't exist.

Renamed the option, and the engine's countryOptions return key, to
priorityCountries throughout the field, the plugin's global config, and the
client options bag. Added an optional priorityCountriesLabel (StaticLabel,
settable at plugin and field level, resolved through resolveStaticLabel the
same way the field's own label is) so an integrator can head the group with
wording they actually chose. With no label configured, no heading renders at
all: the picker's own group divider still marks where the pinned group ends,
so it still reads as distinct from the alphabetized rest, through layout
rather than invented text. The "All countries" heading is gone in every case
too, since once the divider alone carries the split, a second heading naming
the remainder added nothing.

preferredCountries and allCountries are now unreferenced, so both
translation keys are retired from keys.ts and all eleven locale files.

The dev showcase gains priorityFirst (priorityCountries plus a label)
alongside priorityFirstNoLabel, so both renderings are visible side by side.

* docs(fields): document phone priorityCountries and its label

Follows the priorityCountries rename and the new priorityCountriesLabel
option: updates the annotated options block, the country restriction and
pinning section, the plugin-level defaults example, the options table, and
the countryOptions example in the utils reference.

* chore(fields): describe priorityCountries in the phone changeset

The phone number field hasn't released yet, so this isn't a breaking change
to any consumer. The changeset entry now names the option by its final,
priority-based name and mentions priorityCountriesLabel instead of
describing the earlier preferredCountries draft.

* fix(fields): open the phone country picker without scrolling the page

* fix(fields): inset the phone country trigger and centre its chevron

* fix(fields): size the phone country search like a native input

* test(fields): gate flag artwork on every phone entry, not just index.js

index.js reaches flagsEndpoint.js but never CountryFlag.js, so the old
single-entry gate could not see a static `country-flag-icons` import added
to the component the admin actually renders. exports/client.js and
exports/rsc.js are where that regression lands.

Also pins that all five entries really traverse the phone family: walk()
skips an unresolvable specifier, so a truncated graph would otherwise
satisfy every "never statically reaches" assertion vacuously.

* fix(fields): drop an unloadable phone metadata set at the resolver

The read hook and both validators await loadMetadata bare, so a registry
metadata set outside the union rejects there with no degrade path: every
read of the collection and every write fails. normalizeRegistry rejects
one at plugin build time, but a config assembled without the plugin, or
mutated after it ran, reaches the resolver unchecked, which is exactly
the case its docstring claims to cover.

Coerce it to undefined so the documented default applies, and log it.
This also makes the declared `metadata: MetadataSet` return honest: it
was asserting a narrowing the function never performed.

Drops the try/catch and its Proxy test with it. That guard was reachable
only through a throwing getter nobody ships, and did not even cover the
getFieldsRegistry read one line above it, so it gave the name "Safe" a
coverage it never had. The metadata coercion is the failure the name is
actually for.

* docs(fields): state the real reason phone metadata is plugin-level

Both places justified it with a process-wide parser singleton. There is
no singleton: engine/metadata.ts keys a Map per set and every engine
function takes `metadata` as an argument, so a per-field set would work
today. Stated as a technical impossibility it would stop a future
maintainer attempting a cheap change. The decision is the bundle cost.

* refactor(fields): rename PhoneClientOptions to ResolvedPhoneOptions

It is the resolved bag, consumed by three server-only paths, and the
"ClientOptions" suffix already means two different things in this
package: ColorFieldClientOptions is resolved, MeasurementClientOptions
is not.

Narrow the field's own prop to PhoneFieldClientOptions, which omits
cellFormat and validation, and stop shipping them: the client provably
reads neither, and reading validation there would state a verdict the
server has not reached. Free now in beta pre-mode, a major later.

* feat(fields): export countryFlagSrc from /phone

The URL contract lives entirely in that helper: lowercase, encoded,
`.svg` suffix, resolved against the app's own API route. Publishing
FLAGS_PATH alone left a frontend rendering flags to reassemble it and
get a detail wrong. It has no server dependency.

* test(fields): cover the eviction in both phone caches

Both caches evict a rejected promise so a later call retries, and
neither eviction was under test. The existing out-of-union case returns
before the cache is ever written, so deleting the whole .catch left it
green; the flag artwork cache had no case at all. Mock the import to
fail once, assert the rejection, then assert a later call succeeds.

* test(fields): pin every plugin-level phone fallback at once

countries, priorityCountries and priorityCountriesLabel each read
`field.x ?? global?.x` with no case of their own: dropping the global
half of any of the three left the suite green. One populated global
against an empty field layer, compared with toEqual over the whole
resolved bag, covers all three and any key added later.

* test(fields): cover the phone commit that happens before metadata lands

Every committing case flushed the lazy load first, so the branch that
stores the draft verbatim with no parser loaded never ran. Deleting it
left the whole suite green, and it is the field's entire degraded mode.

* test(fields): cover the phone read hook's unparseable guard

Deleting `if (!parsed) return value` made afterRead throw for any row
whose stored number does not parse, which fails the whole request, and
left every test green. Bulk imports and migrations bypass the field's
validation, so that row shape is reachable in practice.

* test(fields): assert the country search autofocuses without scrolling

preventScroll shipped bare. The spy covers the autofocus itself too,
which until now existed only at e2e.

* fix(fields): let a phone country be picked with the mouse

Popup closes itself on any click that reaches a button inside it. Our
rows are buttons, so its native listener on the popup element scheduled
the close, React flushed it at the microtask checkpoint between the two
listeners, and the panel unmounted before React's own delegated handler
on the portal container dispatched the row's onClick. The country never
changed and the panel just closed.

Only real clicks hit it: a dispatched click from a script never reaches
that checkpoint, which is why jsdom and the e2e keyboard path both pass.
Opt the panel out with data-popup-prevent-close; the rows already close
through `select`. Escape, click-outside and Enter all still close.

* test(fields): restore the phone showcase doc in an afterEach

The restore rode on a trailing PATCH inside the test, so a failure
before it left a French number behind and manufactured a second,
misleading failure in the list-view test on the next run. Move the
saving test into its own describe and restore from afterEach.

* test(fields): move three phone checks to the tier that can see them

- Click-select: the unit test drives a stubbed Popup, so it never saw
  the real one closing the panel mid-click. This is the case that found
  that bug, and the only tier that can hold it.
- e164 storage: the one mode writing through setValue rather than

- Picker centring: the unit test proves scrollToIndex was called, not

* fix(fields): degrade a phone read when metadata cannot load

The afterRead hook awaited loadMetadata bare, so one rejected chunk failed the
whole request and took down every read of the collection. It now returns the
stored value and reports through the request logger, matching what the field and
cell server components already do. Both validators keep throwing: swallowing
there would let a write through unvalidated.

* refactor(fields): read a phone value through one validator seam

The object and e164 validators were twelve byte-identical lines apart, differing
only in how the number and its country came out of the value. That difference is
a reader, so there is now one buildValidate taking one, and a third storage shape
costs a reader rather than another copy of the whole body.

* refactor(fields): read phone options through one server helper

The field and cell server components each carried the same ten lines of
prop-or-custom fallback, undefined check and error message, differing only in the
component name. Two copies of a message and a fallback chain are two things to
keep aligned, so they now share readPhoneOptions.

* refactor(fields): build the phone admin components once

The Cell/Field literal was written out twice, identical but for a tab of
indentation, and the isClearable contract was spelled out twice in options. Both
now have one home.

* refactor(fields): drive the phone derived subfields from one list

The five derived names lived in the read hook and again in the group's field
literals, with nothing keeping the two in step: a name added to the hook alone is
written and then silently stripped. One `satisfies keyof ParsedPhone` list now
drives both, which also takes the seven copies of disableListColumn down to one.

* refactor(fields): extract the phone edit model

Eighty-five lines of React-free logic sat at the top of the field component,
reachable only by rendering it: resolveCommit alone takes six arguments and has
seven outcomes. It now lives beside the component as its own module, the way
measurement's does, and the component drops to 373 lines.

* test(fields): cover the phone commit outcomes directly

resolveCommit's seven outcomes were reachable only by rendering the field, so
one of them needed a render that deliberately withheld metadata. Twenty-eight
cases now drive the extracted model straight, one per outcome.

* refactor(fields): couple the phone list height to the row height

The virtualizer measured rows at 34px while the stylesheet capped the list at
272px and the portalled scroll container at 340px, the three held together by
arithmetic and a comment. The list cap is now published from the component off
the same constant, and the outer cap comes off: the panel bounds itself.

* refactor(fields): split the phone draft helpers out of the engine

engine/phone.ts mixed the published engine with admin-input plumbing: ten of its
exports never reach /phone/utils. The barrel drew the line and the isolation spec
held it, but the file did not show it. The typing and row-splitting helpers now
live in engine/draft.ts, which imports the engine and is not imported by it.

* test(fields): close silent-skip gap in dist import walker

walk() dropped an unresolvable relative specifier without a sound, so a
truncated graph could satisfy every "never reaches" assertion in
phone-lazy.spec.ts without having traversed anything. collectUnresolved
surfaces those specifiers instead of swallowing them, and a new assertion
checks the set stays empty across every entry the suite walks, closing
the whole class rather than pinning today's paths alone.

* test(fields): cover popup-close opt-out on CountryPicker

data-popup-prevent-close on the panel root is the entire fix for mouse
selection: without it Popup closes on the click before the row's onClick
fires. Only an e2e spec exercised it, because CountryPicker.test.tsx
drives a hand-rolled popup double that cannot see Payload's real Popup.
A unit assertion now pins the attribute directly, so dropping it while
refactoring the panel fails fast instead of only at the e2e tier.

workflow run while nothing had been reclaimed, and left long workflows covered only by per-task
stamps.

workflow's heartbeat holds the lease for the whole run. Single-task jobs run through Payload's

perf(analytics): rollup and seen-ledger writes are batched per flush

One fully attributed pageview cost 161 driver round trips: 96 rollup upserts
(32 buckets plus a bump per new visitor and session) and 64 ledger inserts,
every one of them awaited in turn. Measured against the same hit, it now costs
4: the event insert, one upsert statement for the base increments, one insert
for the whole ledger batch, and one upsert for the distinct counters. A batch
of N events pays the same three writes, not three per event.

insertManyIfNew answers per row, in order, which of them created its ledger
entry, from Mongo's unordered insertMany write errors and from Postgres's
returning() rows matched back by value. A row repeated inside one batch counts
once on both, since Mongo would raise a duplicate-key error where Postgres
skips silently.

bumpRollups upserts every bucket in one statement (Mongo bulkWrite, Postgres
multi-row ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE reading each row's own increments through
excluded) and sums bumps landing on the same bucket, which Postgres would
otherwise reject as touching a row twice. bumpRollup is now a wrapper on it.

whether the hit counted. All three geo values are capped at MAX_GEO_LENGTH.

of any site's traffic, so counting it would have put a site's own domain at the

and reports nothing for a self-referral; source keeps its own Direct rule.

per render: TrackerBoot's effect may not have run when a sibling renders, and an
eagerly resolved null would never recover. With neither a provider nor a booted
tracker the call still throws, because a silently dead track is worse than a
build-time mistake.

e2e now clicks both buttons and expects both conversions.

names filled both slots with it, and the browser tracker built a sink per slot:
every event went out twice, so one click booked two conversions. One adapter now
fills at most one slot, the global one first.

capture.slots also takes false, so a slot can be left deliberately empty instead
of falling to a default: nothing resolves for it, its proxy mount 404s, and the
tracker config omits it. The goals breakdown defaults to conversions, since
pageviews per goal is a stranger thing to open on.

fetch-on-mount stub, and carries one goal per match kind: a CTA attribute, a
config event name, and a /thank-you path. Both tenancy modes are proven end to
end, the scoped one through an anonymous hostname scope resolver, since public
tracker and ingest calls carry no session.

MeasurementUnitsProvider. Payload drops a provider it cannot resolve along with
everything nested under it, which took the multi-tenant tenant selector with it
and had left all four @tenancy e2e cases red before this change.

flows through.

fix(analytics): harden goal matching and ingest validation

The glob escape class was missing `?`, so a pattern like `/foo?` compiled the
question mark as an optional quantifier and matched `/fo`. Escape every regex
metacharacter but `*`, and put the pattern through the same query/hash cut as
the path it is matched against.

Ingest validation now requires real strings for path, hostname and name: a
non-string path previously reached the path-glob matcher and 500'd instead of
answering 400. The event name is truncated to 128 chars, since it is the `event`
dimension's bucket key.

Revenue only ever counts a finite, non-negative source, so a negative prop or
event value reports 0 rather than subtracting from a bucket, and a configured
`value.fixed` that is negative or non-finite now fails the boot.

The rollup backfill runs one pass per counter so a row half-patched by an
interrupted run is completed without resetting the counters it already carries.

fix(analytics): carry the CSP nonce onto the posthog stub's injected script

The stub injects array.js itself, so under a nonce CSP without
strict-dynamic the nonced inline passed while the bundle it asked for was
blocked. It now copies the nonce of the inline that is running onto the tag
before inserting it, reading `document.currentScript` (the inline itself
during its own synchronous run, on the server-rendered path and the loader's
alike) and preferring the IDL property, since browsers blank the content
attribute once the document is parsed.

Plausible's stub injects nothing of its own and the loader nonces everything
it creates, so neither needed the same treatment; both are pinned by tests.

Also routes `sink.flush()` through the same guard as `sink.send`, so a slot
that throws while flushing cannot skip the slots after it.

`scrollDepth` on any event; optional fields are sanitized and dropped when
malformed rather than failing the event, while a missing type/path/hostname or a
nameless event or goal still 400s.

`matchGoals` (pure) resolves config goals into completions at ingest, under the
same scope the event is stamped with, and the completions are stored on the event
so a filtered or hourly read reports the same numbers the rollups hold.

Rollups gain `conversions`, `revenue`, `scrollDepthSum` and `scrollSamples`; each
completion adds a ('', 'goal', slug) bucket in both hostname families while every
other bucket carries the event's whole conversion count. `scrollDepth` averages
over `scrollSamples` (pageviews that reported a depth), never over `samples`.

`goal` dimension; `AdapterRegisterContext` gains `resolveGoals`.

fix(analytics): sequence vendor snippets with official stubs

The PostHog snippet shipped `array.js` and a bare `posthog.init(...)` as
sibling tags, so whenever the async loader lost the race the inline threw on
an undefined global and nothing was ever published. Both vendors now ship
their own official self-sequencing snippet: PostHog is one inline script
carrying the documented stub, which queues calls and injects array.js itself
off the proxied api_host, and Plausible's per-site inline carries the
`plausible.q` stub that queues calls and parks the endpoint on `plausible.o`
for the tracker to read. Its `init` is guarded with `||`, unlike the official
one, because the loader here is a separate async tag that may win the race.

Vendor sinks now wait for the global rather than for the load promise:
present, dispatch; absent, poll every 100ms for up to 10s after the scripts
load, then drop in silence. Umami has no stub and appears only once its
script has run, which is exactly the case the load promise did not cover.

Covered by a DOM test that runs each snippet for real and asserts the global
it publishes, the script it injects, and that a sink dispatch made before the
SDK lands is queued.

fix(analytics): isolate tracker sinks and gate vendor scripts on consent

Every `sink.send` is guarded, on the dispatch path and on the consent drain,
so a vendor global that throws (or an event that will not serialize) cannot
skip the remaining slots or escape into the host's own click handler.

AnalyticsScripts no longer renders the snippet for a slot that waits for
consent: shipping the script in the HTML ran the vendor's tracker before the
visitor answered, which is what the gate exists to prevent. The slot's sink
injects the same snippet on grant, and the loader skips scripts already in
the page.

React StrictMode mounts an effect, tears it down and mounts it again, so both
components booted two trackers and sent two boot pageviews. They now lease
the window's tracker from a refcounted registry whose teardown is deferred to
a macrotask and skipped when a new holder arrives, so the remount reuses the
instance and a real unmount still destroys it.

Also: restore the history patches only when they are still ours, never
resurrect a provider's tracker after unmount, and treat a blank
data-analytics-value as absent rather than as a zero-revenue conversion.

`/react`. One sink per capture slot: the native sink posts to the config's
ingest path (sendBeacon with a JSON blob, keepalive fetch fallback) and
buffers a pageview until pagehide, the next navigation, or 10s so it carries
durationMs and scroll depth; the vendor sinks load the slot snippet through
the loadScript seam and forward events and goals only, since every vendor
script tracks its own pageviews.

Consent-gated slots queue events (bounded FIFO, 100) until granted, drop them
on denial, and persist the decision in localStorage. Page tracking wraps
history and popstate on a pathname change; auto-capture covers outbound
links, file downloads, scroll thresholds, and data-analytics-goal on click
and submit.

TrackerBoot for the RSC path. Both create the tracker once, in the browser.

the default, so `native({ ingestPath })` no longer sends the browser to an
endpoint that moved.

entry keyed by a runtime provider instance id (`<provider>:<instance>`) skips

override is normalized through the same helper the Next rewrites mount uses,
now a shared leaf module.

resolver that turns them into a TrackerConfig, the public endpoint serving it,
and the RSC that renders each slot's snippet.

The tracker endpoint joins the capture proxy as an unauthenticated caller of the
host's scopeResolver, so a resolver that throws or resolves nothing leaves the
tenant slot absent rather than failing the request. Nothing an adapter keeps
private reaches the response: only capture.client and capture.snippet do, and a
goal's admin-facing name is stripped.

TrackerBoot is a placeholder the tracker package fills in.
fix(analytics): reject root and colliding capture mounts
feat(analytics): captureRewrites from adapter descriptors

fix(analytics): tolerate errored proxy request bodies

A beacon from an unloading tab errors its request stream mid-read, which threw
out of readCappedBody, past the handler's try, into Payload's routeError as a
500 plus an error log. The read loop and the arrayBuffer fallback now catch and
report the body as unreadable, which the handler answers 400 with an empty body,
same as any other malformed request, and nothing is logged.

Distinguishing that from the size cap needs more than a null, so readCappedBody
returns a result union: too-large stays 413, unreadable is the new 400.

Also drops ';' from the path-safe restore set, so it stays percent-encoded
upstream: no vendor path needs it and some upstreams read it as a matrix-param
separator.

fix(analytics): harden the runtime proxy request path

Caps proxied request bodies with a new capture.proxy.maxBodyBytes (default
1 MiB, which clears a PostHog batch carrying session-replay data). A declared
content-length over the cap is refused before a byte is read; a chunked body
declares no length, so the running total is checked per chunk and the read is
cancelled the moment it passes. Either way: 413, nothing forwarded.

The proxy no longer borrows cache.timeoutMs, which is a per-read deadline for
authenticated dashboard queries rather than a public request path. It gets its
own capture.proxy.timeoutMs (default 10s) on a manual AbortController cleared
once fetch resolves, so the deadline covers time-to-headers only and a slow
body streams to completion instead of truncating a healthy 200.

Also: forward if-none-match and if-modified-since so proxied assets can
revalidate; thread descriptor.trailingSlashes through matchProxyRoute instead
of always preserving the slash, and document the contract on ProxyDescriptor
for the rewrites helper; skip a route whose upstream template names a param
its source never produces, which surfaced as a public 500; stop re-encoding
the sub path, which turned legal path characters into escapes the vendor never
sent; answer OPTIONS locally with 204 rather than forwarding a preflight whose
CORS headers we strip; drop the dead stripped-response-header loop.

feat(analytics): first-party runtime proxy endpoint

compiled from the slot adapter's own capture.proxy.routes templates: an
unfilled slot, an adapter without capture, or a path outside the declared
routes answers 404 with an empty body and nothing leaves the server.

Cookies and authorization never go upstream, set-cookie never comes back,
X-Forwarded-For carries the derived client IP or nothing at all, and an
upstream failure or timeout answers 502 without echoing the URL or error.
content-encoding and content-length are dropped from the response: fetch
decodes the body but leaves both describing the compressed bytes.

from the config registry, tenant from the request's own per-scope registry.

fix(webhooks): clear a failed create's secret off the request

`generateOnCreate` stashes the secret it generated on `req.context` and
`revealGeneratedSecret` hands it back once, then clears it. A create that
throws in between never reaches the clear, so the value stays on the
request.

The next create on that same request would then be given the dead secret
as its `generatedSecret`, including one that supplied its own and should
have been handed nothing. A caller who trusted the response would hold a
secret that signs no delivery, and would find out from a receiver
rejecting everything.

REST cannot reach this, since each request creates one document; a Local
API script reusing a `req` across creates can. Clearing on entry rather
than only on success closes it wherever the throw happens.

fix(webhooks): reject an empty secret where it can actually be caught

`secret: ''` on a create returned 201 with no secret stored at all, and
that subscription then delivered unsigned forever. It is the one path
that could produce an unsigned subscription by accident rather than on
purpose, which is precisely the downgrade the refusal path exists to
prevent everywhere else.

An earlier commit meant to fix this by leaving the empty string for the
field validator, and `validateWhsec` was written to pass `''` through
unharmed on the theory that `encryptedField` would reject it. Neither
half was reachable. `encryptedField` seals *before* it validates, and its
seal hook reads a write-only empty string as a clear, so the validator
was handed `null` and saw a subscription that legitimately has no secret.
Nothing rejected anything.

The refusal moves to `generateOnCreate`, a collection `beforeValidate`,
which runs before the field pass and still sees the `''` the caller sent.
`validateWhsec` keeps the tightened guard as a backstop, because admin
form state can reach it without ever running the seal hook, but it is no
longer where the guarantee lives, and both JSDocs now say so.

The new int case sits beside "still sends unsigned when a subscription
legitimately has no secret", since telling those two apart is the whole
point.

exist; the sibling-name assertions it meant are in the collection's test.

refactor(webhooks): store signing secrets with the encrypted field

The storage layer this package grew was the wrong one to keep. It sealed
with `payload.encrypt`, which is aes-256-ctr: no authentication tag, no
key id, a 32-byte key carrying 128 bits, and a `decrypt` that returns
plausible bytes rather than throwing on a wrong key. The `whsec_` shape
check in `decryptSecret` was standing in for the tag the cipher does not
have, and it cannot do that job: it catches random corruption, not a
deliberate edit, and it conflates a wrong key with corrupt data with an
unmigrated legacy value, which is why that one branch had to reason
about three unrelated states at once.

`@10x-media/fields@0.1.0-beta.5` has all of it, so the storage layer
comes out. `src/secrets/crypto.ts` and `src/secrets/revealWindow.ts` are
gone entirely, along with `maskSecret`, the create-time reveal stash, and
the SECRET_MASK / SECRET_UNUSABLE / CIPHER_PREFIX / SECRET_REVEAL_CONTEXT
constants. `format.ts` is untouched: `whsec_` normalization and the key
derivation are about the Standard Webhooks wire format, not storage.

Both slots are `protection: 'writeOnly'` under a pinned aadScope. The
scope is pinned because the subscriptions slug is a plugin option and the
default binding is that slug, so a consumer renaming the collection would
otherwise turn every stored secret into an authentication failure nothing
could recover. `secretEncryption.keys` passes a key ring straight
through, which makes changing PAYLOAD_SECRET one config line instead of a
capture-and-restore script.

Write-only strips the field from every read, the create response
included, so a generated secret comes back under `generatedSecret` from
an afterChange; that contract change is in the changeset. The delivery
path reads deliberately instead: one `withRawEncrypted` query for the
listening rows, `decryptFieldValue` per row, and `readEncryptedField`
inside the rotation transaction. A failed decrypt now arrives typed, so
the single "could not be decrypted" branch becomes three messages that
each name a different fix. The refusal itself is unchanged, and a
`hidden` slot still separates "no secret configured" from "nobody opened
the raw window", which write-only makes indistinguishable otherwise and
which would be a silent downgrade to unsigned.

Two bugs surfaced on the way. Payload merges the stored document into
`data`, so a duplicate arrived carrying the original's sealed secret and
two subscriptions ended up sharing one signing key; a sealed value on a
create is now treated as absent. The same merge meant the lapsed-rotation
cleanup's `data.previousSecret !== undefined` guard was always true, so
it had never once fired.

The Signing secret field is create-only. `WriteOnlyField` does not
consult Payload's `readOnly`, so its Replace and Generate actions
rendered over a field whose `update` access denies the write: an operator
could type a new secret, save, see no error, and still be signing with
the old one. Rotation is the only way to change a stored secret and now
has the only control.

Alongside: Content-Type and User-Agent join the reserved header set,
since the body is always JSON and a relabelled delivery is unnoticeable
from the receiving end; `webhook-id` becomes an opaque `msg_<id>` rather
than a SQL adapter's sequential row key; the dispatcher narrows on the
event in the `where` and skips the raw window entirely in queue mode,
where it was decrypting only to throw the plaintext away; both
collections take `overrides`; header names are checked against RFC 9110's
token grammar rather than failing at delivery; `rotate.ts` reads
`result.errors` before treating an empty `docs` as a conflict; and
`beginRotation` warns when the adapter opens no transaction instead of
degrading silently.

The rotation UI moves off `window.confirm` and a 60-second toast onto
Payload's own modal chrome, with a copy that falls back to a
selection-based one outside a secure context and an explicit
acknowledgement. The button no longer renders for a user the collection's
update access denies, and the document refreshes so the new grace window
is visible.

The matrix now covers the rotation lifecycle, the grace window in both
its stored shapes, and the event narrowing on both databases; the rotate
button gets e2e coverage; and "the secret is locked against updates" is
asserted against the stored row rather than against the config shape.

fix(webhooks): give rotation snapshot isolation on sql adapters

The conditional write was not the guarantee it looked like. Payload
resolves a `where` to ids with a SELECT and then updates each row by id,
in both updateOne and updateMany, so the check and the act are separate
statements. Under Postgres' default READ COMMITTED both rotations match
the same row, and once the first commits the second overwrites it and
reports success to a caller whose secret is already gone. The compare-
and-swap read as atomic and was not.

The rotation transaction now opens at REPEATABLE READ where the adapter
is a SQL one, which turns that second write into a serialization failure
the endpoint already reports as a 409. Mongo keeps its own options: its
transactions are snapshot-isolated and abort the loser already, which the
matrix has been proving all along, and its adapter takes an unrelated
options shape. `drizzle` marks the SQL adapters rather than a list of
names. The `where` guard stays as the check for an adapter with no
transactions at all.

The matrix case was also asserting against `Promise.allSettled` order,
which is input order and says nothing about which rotation committed
last. It now records each secret as its rotation resolves and compares
the active secret against that, and separately asserts the shape a lost
update leaves behind: the pre-rotation secret still sitting in the grace
window after two rotations both succeeded. That second assertion is the
one that fails without the isolation level, on every run.

docs(webhooks): point at the csrf allowlist for cross-site protection

A review asked for a bespoke CSRF check on the rotate endpoint. Payload
already covers it: extractJWT validates a cookie-authenticated request
against `config.csrf`, or falls back to `Sec-Fetch-Site` when no Origin is
sent, and that runs before `req.user` exists. Rotation is therefore no
weaker than the collection's own update endpoint, and a check only there
would break non-browser clients while leaving every other mutation open.

What is worth saying is that the allowlist is empty by default, so the
security page now says so and shows how to set it.

test(webhooks): isolate the header cases and stop hardcoding constants

Two header assertions read a `received` captured by an earlier test, so
they asserted against a stale delivery and passed vacuously whenever they
ran alone or the order changed. Each now sends its own delivery.

assertion cannot leak it into the next test; pin the newest row in the
queue-path lookup the way its own helper already does; use CIPHER_PREFIX,
SECRET_MASK and SECRET_REVEAL_CONTEXT rather than repeating their values;

snippet drifts, which it cannot do: nothing links the two. It now says

feat(webhooks): confirm before rotating, and say why a rotation failed

The button rotated on a single click. Rotation is destructive from the
receiver's side, since it starts the clock on the secret they are using
right now and there is no undo, so it asks first. Cancelling makes no
request and leaves the button enabled.

Failures also collapsed into one "could not rotate the secret" regardless
of cause, which hid three different next steps behind one message: a
permission problem, a secret the server would not accept, and a
concurrent rotation that just needs retrying. Each status now maps to its
own message, with the generic one kept for anything unexpected.

Verified both paths against the running dev app: cancelling fires no
request, and accepting still reveals the new secret once.

fix(webhooks): reject an explicitly empty secret on create

`data.secret ? normalize : generate` treated an empty string as no secret
at all, so a caller who sent `secret: ""` got a generated one instead and
an HTTP 201. They never saw the value, and the subscription signed with a
secret they did not have, which surfaces later as a receiver rejecting
every delivery rather than as the 400 it should have been.

Only undefined and null generate now. Payload's admin omits the field
rather than sending it empty, verified against the running dev app, so
this is API callers only.

fix(webhooks): restore the previous reveal flag instead of clearing it

All three internal reads opened a reveal window and then forced the flag
to `false` on the way out, rather than putting back what was there. Any
nesting therefore closed a window the outer caller was still relying on,
and the next read on that request saw the mask instead of key material.
Until recently a masked secret meant an unsigned delivery, and it now
means a refused one, so either way the damage is silent and lands far
from the call that caused it.

withRevealWindow captures and restores the flag, and the three sites go
through it, so a future nested read is safe by construction rather than
by each caller remembering.

fix(webhooks): make rotation safe against a concurrent rotation

The transaction alone only covered Mongo, which aborts one side of a
contended write. Under Postgres' default READ COMMITTED, two rotations
can both read the same secret and the second write simply lands on top of
the first: the first caller has already been handed a secret that now
signs nothing, and the secret both of them retired is one that is already
gone. No error is raised on either side.

The write is now conditional on the stored secret the read saw, which is
a compare-and-swap Payload can express through an ordinary `where` and so
works the same on both databases. A rotation whose row moved underneath
it raises RotationConflictError, which the endpoint already maps to 409
alongside driver-level write conflicts, so the caller retries and reads
the winner's secret rather than overwriting it.

Reading the stored form rather than the decrypted one gives the swap
token and the outgoing plaintext from a single read, so the two cannot
describe different values. graceSeconds is validated here as well, since
a direct caller bypasses the endpoint that used to be the only guard.

The cross-db matrix covers it: the new case fails on postgres without the
conditional write, and passes on both with it.

refactor(webhooks): let decryptSecret own ciphertext validity

isEncryptedSecret checked the tag and then re-validated the ciphertext
body, which split the question of what a valid ciphertext is across two
places and got the tagged-but-corrupt case backwards: it answered "not
encrypted", so a corrupt value was sent back through the cipher a second
time on the next write instead of being reported as unreadable. The tag
is the whole test now, and decryptSecret decides recoverability.

The untagged fallback also warns once per process. A well-formed but
untagged secret is one that predates encryption at rest: signing with it
keeps the subscription working, which is why the fallback exists, but it
is plaintext in the database and nothing said so. The secret itself is
never logged.

fix(webhooks): reject non-canonical base64 secrets

The group-structure check pinned the length but not the encoding. Base64
does not require the final group's unused low bits to be zero, so
`AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA==` and `AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAB==` are different
strings that decode to byte-identical key material. Both were accepted
and stored verbatim, so one key could exist under two names: rotation
compares secrets as strings, so rotating from one spelling to the other
looked like a real rotation while the HMAC key never changed.

Round-tripping the decoded bytes and requiring an exact match pins one
spelling per key. Generated secrets are canonical already, and a legacy
hex secret still normalizes unchanged.

fix(webhooks): refuse a masked active secret instead of sending unsigned

The resolver treated a masked active secret exactly like an absent one:
both produced no signing keys and a clear `secretUnusable`, so the
delivery went out with no `webhook-signature` header at all. The mask
means something quite different from absence, though. It says a secret
exists and this read simply never opened the signing reveal window, so
the case it actually covers is a delivery path that forgot
`SECRET_REVEAL_CONTEXT.forSigning` - and the result was the silent
downgrade to unsigned that the rest of this work exists to prevent.

Slots now carry a state rather than a boolean, so absent, masked and
unusable stay distinct. A masked active secret refuses the delivery with
its own reason, a genuinely secretless subscription still delivers
unsigned as before, and a masked retired secret stays benign because the
active secret already carries the delivery. sendDelivery grows the
matching backstop.

fix(webhooks): name the subscription in decrypt-failure logs

Both decrypt-failure messages said a secret could not be decrypted
without saying whose. An install with more than a handful of
subscriptions got one such error per delivery attempt with nothing in it
to identify the row that needs migrating or rotating, which is the one
piece of information the operator needs to act.

The field hook already receives `collection` and `originalDoc`, so the
messages now carry the collection slug and the document id.

fix(webhooks): keep the required check on custom header names

A field's custom `validate` replaces Payload's built-in validation rather
than running alongside it, so `required: true` on the header name was
inert: the validator returned `true` for undefined, null and empty
strings, and only rejected reserved names. A header row saved with no
name reached the delivery pipeline, where `rowHeaders` skipped it.

The validator now rejects an empty name itself, using Payload's own
`validation:required` so the message matches every other required field,
and the reserved-name message moves to a typed translation key with the
offending name interpolated, per the repo's typed-i18n rule.

fix(webhooks): scope the signing refusal to the secret that must work

The refusal that replaced the unsigned downgrade was too broad. It keyed
off a single flag covering both secret slots, so a *retired* secret that
could not be decrypted failed every delivery for that subscription, even
though the current secret was fine and a fully valid signature was
available. That trades a correctly signed delivery for no delivery at
all, with no security gain: the reasoning behind the refusal is that a
signed subscription must never be sent unsigned, and signing with the
current secret satisfies it.

The two slots are now resolved apart. `secretUnusable` still refuses when
the active secret is unrecoverable; `retiredSecretUnusable` drops the
retired one and delivers, losing only the rotation overlap. The mask
hook takes its slot so the log says which happened, rather than warning
that deliveries will fail when they will not.

This also fixed a documented procedure that produced a dead subscription.
The `PAYLOAD_SECRET` runbook captured and restored `secret` alone, so a
subscription mid-rotation kept a retired secret encrypted under the old
key and, under the old behaviour, stayed dead for the rest of its window.
The runbook now carries both fields across, and the partial case degrades
to a working delivery instead of none.

Smaller fixes found in the same pass:

- **Duplicate returned 400.** Payload's duplicate action resubmits a
  document it read, so the create saw the mask where a secret would be
  and rejected it as malformed key material. Placeholders are treated as
  absent on create, giving the copy its own fresh secret, and dropped on
  write rather than only the mask being dropped.
- **Retired secrets were never cleared.** A lapsed grace window is inert
  but stayed in the row forever. It is now nulled on the row's next
  write, which needs no scheduler and cannot race a delivery.
- **A thrown `Forbidden` became a 500.** Throwing is as valid a denial as
  returning false, and Payload's own `executeAccess` lets it propagate,
  so the rotate endpoint reported it as a server error. It maps to 403.
- **The reveal window relied on cleanup that never ran.** Payload invokes
  collection `afterError` from its HTTP layer only, so a Local API create
  that threw after `beforeChange` reached neither hook. The stash is
  consumed on first match instead, closing the window at the read.
- **Non-canonical base64 was accepted.** A ragged length decoded its
  leftover bits away, so a clipped paste silently became a shorter key
  and two different strings could derive the same one.
- **Migration reporting.** Rows with no secret counted as already
  encrypted, and one unusable field stranded its recoverable sibling in
  plaintext. Failures now name the field, a row migrates what it can, and
  `noSecret` is counted separately.
- **Docs.** The quick-start receiver lacked the try/catch that turns a
  forged request into a 400 rather than a 500; the hand-rolled verifier
  ignored the `v1` tag; redelivery's fresh `webhook-id` and what it means
  for receiver idempotency was undocumented; the changeset still
  described the removed unsigned fallback.

The rotate endpoint's guards were covered by tests asserting only that an
access function existed and that the endpoint was registered, leaving
authorization, body validation and status mapping unexercised. Those are
replaced by tests that drive the handler.

fix(webhooks): guard the rotate endpoint's input, access, and concurrency

Four problems with rotation, all in the path between the request and the
write.

**Authorization was login only.** The handler checked `req.user` and then
rotated with `overrideAccess: true`, so a consumer who tightened
`access.update` on the subscriptions collection still had an open rotate
endpoint, and any authenticated user could rotate any subscription and
receive the new plaintext, breaking that receiver. It now evaluates the
collection's configured `update` access for the target document, honouring
a `Where` result by checking the document matches it. Tenant scoping that
access will govern rotation for free.

**`graceSeconds` from the body was unvalidated.** The configured value is
checked at config build, but the per-request override went straight
through. An unbounded value kept the retired secret signing for
millennia, the opposite of what rotating after an exposure is for; a
non-numeric one failed `graceSeconds > 0` and retired the old secret
instantly with no window and no error. The body is now parsed, and both
paths share `resolveSecretRotationOptions`, which gained a 30-day ceiling.

**Rotation was an unguarded read-modify-write.** Two rotations whose reads
both landed before either write both retired the same original secret, and
the loser's new secret was discarded after its caller had already been
handed it as theirs. Read and write now share a transaction.

**Failures surfaced as driver internals.** A write conflict escaped the
handler's `InvalidSecretError`-only catch and reached the client as a 500
carrying a MongoServerError message. Conflicts are now 409 with a retry
hint, and anything else is logged and returned as a generic 500.

Docs also record that only the most recently retired secret is kept, so a
second rotation inside an open window ends the first secret's grace period
early. That was deliberate and asserted by a test, but undocumented while
the docs promised the old secret worked until its window closed.

fix(webhooks): scope the create reveal to the field and document it belongs to

The reveal stash was a bare plaintext string on `req.context`, and the
mask hook was registered on both secret fields, so under an open reveal
window it returned that plaintext for whichever field was being read.
The create response echoed the new secret a second time as
`previousSecret`, which is both an unadvertised reveal channel and simply
wrong data.

`clearRevealOnce` also only runs on a successful `afterChange`, so a
create that threw after `beforeChange` left the window open for the rest
of the request. A later read of a different subscription on the same
request then returned the failed create's plaintext in place of the mask.
A REST request boundary limited that, but a job run or a nested Local API
call does not, and a shared job request becomes a cross-tenant concern
once tenancy lands.

The stash now carries the ciphertext it was stored as, and a reveal
requires the value being read to equal it. Every encryption uses a fresh
IV, so a stash can only match the document it came from: one left behind
by a failed create is inert rather than dangerous. That is a structural
guarantee rather than a cleanup that has to run, though `afterError` now
clears the window too. The mask hook takes the field's reveal capability
explicitly, and `previousSecret` never reveals.

fix(webhooks): never send unsigned, never store a secret in plaintext

Two ways the encryption work could be bypassed, both in the paths that
decide what a stored secret means.

**An undecryptable secret silently downgraded the delivery to unsigned.**
A signing read returned null, the resolver dropped it, and sendDelivery
omitted the `webhook-signature` header entirely, so the request went out
and the row was recorded `success`. Receivers written as "verify if a
signature header is present", a very common shape, accept those
unconditionally.

The blast radius was every subscription created before encryption at
rest. An unmigrated legacy secret is unprefixed, fails the decrypt path's
`whsec_` check, and reads back as null, so from the moment this branch
deployed those subscriptions delivered unsigned until
encryptExistingSecrets was run by hand. One log line was the only signal.

The root cause is that null conflated "no secret configured", where
unsigned is correct, with "a secret exists but is unusable", where it is
not. A signing read that cannot recover a secret now yields
SECRET_UNUSABLE, `ResolvedSubscription` carries `secretUnusable`, and
`decideDelivery` refuses: the row is marked `dead` with an explicit
reason and nothing is POSTed. sendDelivery throws on the flag as a
backstop so a future call site cannot reintroduce the downgrade by
forgetting the check. Rotation still recovers a broken subscription: the
sentinel is nothing to carry into a grace period rather than a value to
store as the previous secret.

**`previousSecret` supplied on create was persisted as plaintext.** The
create branch never ran it through the encrypt path, and the field denied
only update, not create, so an ordinary REST or GraphQL create wrote a
plaintext `whsec_` value straight to the database. `admin.hidden` hides a
field in the UI and gates nothing. Since a plaintext secret decrypts to
itself, a caller could also plant a second, permanent signing key of
their choosing on any subscription they created. Both rotation fields now
deny create as well as update, and the create branch encrypts
`previousSecret` too, so an `overrideAccess` write cannot store plaintext
either.

security.mdx and the changeset described the old unsigned fallback as
